draft.title: Problem-solution and compare-contrast structures
card: Problem-solution
The writer first explains a problem and why it matters. Then the writer sets out one or more solutions to it.
Compare-contrast
The writer looks at the likenesses (compare) and the differences (contrast) between two things. Each point is dealt with for both things before moving to the next point.
Problem-solution texts often use words such as issue, because, so, one answer and as a result. Compare-contrast texts often use similarly, in the same way, however, whereas and on the other hand.
A structure shapes how a reader follows the ideas. A problem-solution text leads towards a fix. A compare-contrast text helps a reader weigh two things side by side.
draft.remember: Problem-solution moves from a problem to answers. Compare-contrast sets two things side by side, point by point.

a.q: A paragraph begins: Many students arrive at school tired. It then suggests a later start time and a rule about screens at night. Which structure is it?
opts: Problem-solution, but only if it has a heading
Compare-contrast, but only if it names two schools
a.why: The paragraph names a problem, tired students, and then offers answers to it. That is problem-solution. It does not set two things side by side, so it is not compare-contrast.
a.clue: Does the writer set out a trouble and then fixes for it?

b.q: A writer discusses cost, comfort and speed for trains, then cost, comfort and speed for buses, using whereas and similarly. How is the text organised?
opts: Problem-solution, with a clear problem first
Compare-contrast, with all trains first then all buses
b.why: The writer takes each point, such as cost, and looks at both trains and buses before moving on. That is compare-contrast point by point. Nothing in the text is a problem that needs solving, so problem-solution is wrong.
b.clue: Look at the linking words and at what the writer covers for both things.

b.best: Compare-contrast, with all trains first then all buses

problems.detail: The stem says the writer covers cost, comfort and speed for trains, then cost, comfort and speed for buses. That is a block (all of one, then all of the other) structure, not point by point. The intended answer 'Compare-contrast, point by point' is wrong for the stem as written. The option 'Compare-contrast, with all trains first then all buses' matches it.

The why says the writer takes each point, such as cost, and looks at both trains and buses before moving on. This contradicts the question stem, which describes all of trains first, then all of buses.

The card defines compare-contrast as always dealing with each point for both things before moving on. Compare-contrast texts can also use a block structure, covering one thing fully and then the other. Question b's distractor relies on that structure, yet the card presents point by point as the only way.

proposal.title: Problem-solution and compare-contrast structures
card: Problem-solution
The writer first explains a problem and why it matters, then sets out one or more solutions. Words such as issue, because and as a result often signal it.
Compare-contrast
The writer looks at the likenesses (compare) and the differences (contrast) between two things. Words such as similarly, however and whereas often signal it.
Point by point
takes one point, such as cost, and covers both things before moving to the next point. A block structure instead covers all of one thing, then all of the other.
A structure shapes how a reader follows the ideas. A problem-solution text leads towards a fix. A compare-contrast text helps a reader weigh two things against each other.
proposal.remember: Problem-solution moves from a problem to its fixes. Compare-contrast weighs two things, point by point or in blocks.

a.q: A paragraph begins: Many students arrive at school tired. It then suggests a later start time and a rule about screens at night. Which structure is it?
opts: Problem-solution, from a problem to its fixes
Compare-contrast, two start times side by side
Problem-solution, from fixes back to a problem
a.why: The paragraph names a problem first, tired students, and then offers ways to fix it. That is problem-solution in its usual order. The fixes come after the problem, not before it, and the writer is not weighing two things against each other.
a.clue: What does the paragraph start with, and what follows?

b.q: A writer compares trains and buses. One paragraph covers the cost of both, the next the comfort of both, then the speed of both. How is it organised?
b.why: Each paragraph takes one point and covers both trains and buses before moving on. That is compare-contrast, point by point. A block structure would cover everything about trains first, then everything about buses.
b.clue: Does each paragraph cover one thing, or one point for both things?
